Well, I've been farming these 5 mu for 15 years now, and I know every corner of this land. My wife and I do most of the work. My son and his wife work over in the county town at a small factory, so they send some money home when they can, but they can't get off work during busy season. We have two grandkids in school, so we need cash for fees and books. That means I have to watch every yuan.

It's almost October, so I need to get the wheat in the ground soon. I usually plant around October 8th. I buy improved wheat seed from the shop in town — I don't save my own seed because the yield drops, and at 5 mu I only need about 100 kg total, which costs me roughly 350–400 yuan. I use whatever variety the dealer says is doing well locally, usually Jinmai or something similar. After the maize comes off, I plow the field, then harrow it fine before planting.

For fertilizer, the extension technician came by last spring and said 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is about right for my soil, but last year I used a bit more than that and got a good yield, around 450 kg per mu, so I'll stick with about the same. I put down 40 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) before planting — that's what I can afford for the base. Then in late March, when the wheat starts greening up, I'll topdress with about 18 kg of urea per mu if the plants look a bit yellow. That brings me to roughly 15 kg N per mu total. I know some of the bigger farms use more, but with school fees to pay, I can't push it.

Irrigation is where I count my money most carefully. Pumping water from the well costs me about 30–35 yuan per mu each time. I always do the freezing water in early December so the wheat survives the winter. Then I irrigate once at jointing in late March. If it rains well in April and early May, I'll skip the grain-filling irrigation — that's 150–175 yuan saved on 5 mu, and honestly the yield difference isn't always worth being short of cash if someone gets sick.

For pesticides, I spray herbicide once in early spring — the wild oats and chenopodium are bad on my land. I keep a bottle of fungicide in the shed in case rust shows up, but I only spray if I actually see spots on the leaves.

For maize, the window is brutal. We harvest wheat around June 12th, and I need that maize in the ground by June 14th or I'm in real trouble. I hire the rotary tiller guy to come the same afternoon — costs about 30 yuan per mu — and I plant the next morning. I buy hybrid seed, usually Zhengdan 958 or whatever the dealer recommends, about 3–4 kg per mu. That runs me about 250–300 yuan for the 5 mu. I put 35 kg of compound fertilizer in the row at planting, and then topdress with about 18 kg of urea at the big trumpet stage in late July. Total N comes to about 14 kg per mu — a little less than what the technician writes in his pamphlet, but it's what I can manage and it has worked for me.

Maize irrigation depends entirely on the sky. If June and July give us normal rains, maybe I don't pump at all. But I almost always have to irrigate once at tasseling in late July or early August. If it's really dry, I'll pump twice, but I hate seeing that electricity bill.

Labor is mostly us. My wife and I can handle the planting, fertilizing, and spraying. At wheat harvest, the custom combine cuts the crop in half a day, but we still need to bag and haul it. I might hire one neighbor for a day to help move the bags if my son can't get off work — that's 150 yuan. Maize harvest is all machine now, so no hired labor there.

I expect about 420 kg per mu for wheat if we don't get a late frost, and about 480 kg per mu for maize. Those are decent years for me. Total input costs — seed, fertilizer, irrigation, pesticide, and that one day of hired help — will run me about 3,200 yuan for the whole year on these 5 mu. That's a big chunk of cash to find at planting time, but if both crops do okay, we'll have enough to eat and pay the school fees.
